rig.fx_volume_desc: swells and level, great with an expression pedal

rig.fx_transparent_desc: more of your sound, a little hairier
rig.fx_harmonic_trem_desc: lows and highs pulse in turns
rig.how_gate: A noise gate mutes the signal when it falls below the threshold, so hiss and hum disappear between phrases. Release sets how fast it closes after you stop.
rig.how_volume: A volume pedal only scales the level. Early in the chain it works like your guitar's volume knob; after the drive it fades the whole sound.
rig.how_compressor: A compressor turns loud notes down and lets quiet ones through, so everything sounds even and sustains longer. Attack sets how much of the pick's snap passes before it reacts; blend mixes back the uncompressed signal.
rig.how_opto_comp: Optical compressors control the gain with a light and a light sensor. The sensor reacts slowly and lets go even more slowly, so the squeeze is smooth and hard to hear.
rig.how_boost: A boost raises the level without clipping on its own. Before a driven amp it pushes the amp harder; tilt brightens or darkens on the way.
rig.how_overdrive: This overdrive cuts the lows before its soft clipper and adds them back clean afterwards, so the distortion stays tight and the mids stand out.
rig.how_transparent: A transparent drive mixes your clean signal with a lightly clipped copy. Your guitar's character and low end stay, with some extra grit on top.
rig.how_asym_drive: The mids are boosted before an asymmetric clipper: the top and bottom of the wave are flattened differently, which adds even harmonics and a warm, vocal sound.
rig.how_distortion: Hard clipping flattens the wave sharply into something close to a square: lots of sustain and odd harmonics. The tone control is a low-pass filter after it.
rig.how_fuzz: A fuzz drives a very high-gain stage with a slight offset, so the wave turns into a fuzzy square that breaks up when the note decays.
rig.how_octave_fuzz: Folding the negative half of the wave up (full-wave rectifying) doubles its frequency: an octave above. A fuzz stage after it squares the result off.
rig.how_wah: A wah is a resonant band-pass filter whose center moves: with your foot (manual) or following how hard you play (auto).
rig.how_envelope: An envelope follower measures how loud you play and moves a resonant low-pass filter with it: picking hard opens it (up) or closes it (down).
rig.how_eq: A graphic EQ has one fixed filter per band. Raising or cutting a band changes only that part of the spectrum.
rig.how_chorus: A chorus mixes your signal with a copy delayed a few milliseconds, with the delay slowly moving. The tiny pitch wobble sounds like several players.
rig.how_flanger: A flanger uses an even shorter moving delay with feedback, so the comb of cancellations sweeps up and down: the jet-plane sound.
rig.how_phaser: A phaser runs the signal through all-pass filters that shift phase, and mixes it back: notches appear and sweep slowly through the spectrum.
rig.how_tremolo: A tremolo turns the volume up and down with a low-frequency oscillator. The shape decides whether it pulses smoothly or chops.
rig.how_harmonic_trem: The signal is split into lows and highs, and each half pulses in the opposite phase. The volume barely changes, but the tone moves.
rig.how_vibrato: A vibrato is a moving delay with no dry signal: you only hear the copy, so the pitch itself wobbles.
rig.how_rotary: A rotating speaker throws the highs from a spinning horn and the lows from a slower drum. The movement adds pitch wobble and volume swirl, and changing speed takes a moment.
rig.how_ring_mod: A ring modulator multiplies your signal by a sine wave. Instead of your notes you hear their sum and difference with that frequency: metallic and out of key on purpose.
rig.how_octaver: An octaver tracks the pitch you play and adds a synthesized note one or two octaves below.
rig.how_pitch: A pitch shifter reads the signal in short slices and replays them faster or slower, so everything moves by a fixed interval.
rig.how_delay: A delay plays your signal back later; feedback sends the echo back in for more repeats. Analog and tape modes darken each repeat, like the old machines.
rig.how_reverb: A reverb adds the thousands of reflections of a room, hall, plate or spring. Decay is how long they last.
rig.how_capture: A captured amp is a drive curve and an EQ fitted from two recordings: your guitar straight in and the same playing through the amp. It's an approximation, not the real circuit.

signal.title: Signal check
signal.subtitle: A few minutes to get your guitar sounding right for guitarr: noise, knobs, interface gain and how your notes are heard.
signal.silence_lead: Rest your hand on the strings so nothing rings, don't play, and press Measure. This is the noise guitarr will have to ignore.
signal.noise_quiet: Quiet: the noise floor is {{db}} dB. 👍
signal.noise_some_noise: Some noise: {{db}} dB. It works, but it could be cleaner.
signal.noise_noisy: A lot of noise: {{db}} dB while you're not playing.
signal.noise_tip_gain: If the input gain is very high, the noise goes up with it: the next steps help you set it.
signal.noise_tip_mute: Make sure all the strings are muted while measuring.
signal.hum_found: There's mains hum at {{hz}} Hz (a buzz under everything).
signal.hum_tip_charger: Unplug the laptop charger and measure again: it's the most common cause (a ground loop).
signal.hum_tip_touch: Touch the strings or the bridge: if it gets quieter, it's a grounding issue.
signal.hum_tip_pickup: Single-coil pickups hum more: try the middle position or a humbucker.
signal.hum_tip_cable: Try another cable and move away from screens, lamps and power supplies.
signal.guitar_lead: Before setting levels, check these. They make the biggest difference with an electric guitar.
signal.chk_volume: Guitar volume all the way up
signal.chk_volume_why: you'll control the level on the interface, not on the guitar
signal.chk_tone_why: a closed tone hides the attacks guitarr listens for
signal.chk_pickup_why: brighter and clearer attacks than the neck pickup
signal.chk_inst: INST / Hi-Z input on the interface
signal.chk_inst_why: an electric guitar needs it; on a line input it sounds weak and dull
signal.chk_autogain_why: they squash the attacks (check the interface or USB cable app)
signal.chk_direct_why: no pedals or amp sims before it: guitarr's effects come after the listener
signal.gain_lead: Strum hard, again and again, and turn the gain knob on your interface until the arrow says you're there. You'll hear a chime when it's right.
signal.level_too_low: Too low (peaks at {{db}} dB): raise the gain about {{change}} dB.
signal.level_too_hot: Too hot (peaks at {{db}} dB): lower the gain about {{change}} dB.
signal.level_clipping: It's clipping: lower the gain about {{change}} dB.
signal.level_no_signal: No signal: check the cable, the input and the channel.
signal.level_limited: Something is squashing your signal: the attacks barely stand out.
signal.level_detail: Peak {{peak}} dB · attack {{crest}} dB above the sustained sound (a clean guitar: 15–20 dB)
signal.limited_tip_1: Turn off any auto-gain, limiter or compressor on the interface (or in its app / the USB cable's settings).
signal.limited_tip_2: Unplug pedals or amp simulators between the guitar and the interface.
signal.limited_tip_3: Lower the gain: some interfaces compress when driven hard.
signal.notes_lead: Play the {{n}} open strings one at a time, softly, from the thickest, letting each ring about a second. guitarr will find the settings that hear exactly those notes.
signal.found_settings: Best settings: noise gate {{gate}} dB · sensitivity {{sens}}
signal.too_many: It hears extra notes: mute the strings after each note and play a bit cleaner, then record again.
signal.too_few: Some notes were missed: play a little harder or leave more space between notes, then record again.
signal.needs_tuning: Some strings are out of tune (shown in cents).
signal.listen_lead: This is exactly what guitarr hears. Listen with headphones: hum, distortion or a squashed sound are easy to spot.
signal.nothing_recorded: Nothing recorded for that step yet
signal.done_lead: These settings are made for your guitar and your interface. You can run the check again any time.

warmup.rule: Play it clean ({{need}}% or more) at the goal tempo or faster and the goal goes up {{by}} BPM. Each drill keeps its own goal.
warmup.kept: {{score}}%: the goal stays at {{goal}} BPM (it rises from {{need}}%). Clean before fast.
warmup.spider_focus: Finger independence and hands in sync
warmup.spider_why: The classic warm-up: one finger per fret makes all four fingers work evenly, and alternate picking has to land together with the fretting hand. It gets the hand ready to play by position, which is how the scales and arpeggios of the other drills work.
warmup.spider_how: One finger per fret (1-2-3-4) on each string, from the lowest string to the highest and back down on the same frets. Alternate picking. Start 10–20 BPM under what you can do: no muffled notes.
warmup.pentatonic_focus: The most used scale in rock and blues, in its five boxes
warmup.pentatonic_why: The minor pentatonic is the basic vocabulary of solos. Studying one box a day links the whole neck: where one box ends the next begins, as in CAGED. Saying the degrees (1, ♭3, 4, 5, ♭7) as you play fixes the theory in your fingers.
warmup.pentatonic_how: Two notes per string, up and down the whole box. Keep the hand still in the position; the roots are your landmarks.
warmup.major: Major scale, three notes per string
warmup.major_focus: The ruler of all theory, in seven positions
warmup.major_why: The major scale is the ruler for everything: degrees, intervals, chords and harmony come out of it. Three notes per string keeps the fingering regular, and each position starts on a different degree, covering the neck.
warmup.major_how: Three notes on each string, up and down. Use 1-2-4 for whole step + whole step and 1-3-4 for half step + whole step; slide the hand without breaking the metronome's pulse.
warmup.arpeggios_focus: Seeing 1, 3 and 5 in the E, A and D shapes
warmup.arpeggios_why: An arpeggio is the chord note by note: what you use to solo over each chord. Going up the major and down the minor in the same shape shows that only the 3rd changes (3 → ♭3).
warmup.arpeggios_how: Up the major arpeggio, down the minor one, without moving the hand. Root and 5th stay put; only the 3rd drops a half step.
warmup.octaves_focus: Picking-hand aim and the octave shape
warmup.octaves_why: The octave shape is the fastest way to find a note anywhere, and playing it skipping a string trains the picking hand's aim and the muting of the string in between.
warmup.octaves_how: Low note, then its octave two strings up, climbing fret by fret. Mute the middle string with the fretting finger lying lightly on it.
warmup.caged_focus: The five chord shapes as arpeggios
warmup.caged_why: CAGED links the whole neck with five chord shapes that fit into each other. Playing each shape's notes as an arpeggio, you start seeing the chord (and the scale around it) anywhere, not only in the barre you already know.
warmup.caged_how: Play the chord tones of the shape from the lowest to the highest and back. Then try the next shape up the neck.
warmup.legato_focus: Hammer-ons and pull-offs, even and in time
warmup.legato_why: Legato makes phrases flow like a voice and frees the picking hand. Doing it in time, with the slurred notes as loud as the picked ones, is what makes it sound musical instead of sloppy.
warmup.legato_how: Pick only the first note on each string: hammer up to the second, pull off coming down. Mute the strings you're not playing.
warmup.sweep_focus: One pick motion across the strings, every note on its own
warmup.sweep_why: Sweeping plays an arpeggio with one stroke across the strings. The hard part is the fretting hand: each note has to sound alone, not ring into a chord.
warmup.sweep_how: Down strokes going toward the high strings, up strokes coming back. Lift each finger right after its note. Start slow, three strings at a time if you need to.
